articles.title: 'It Was Pretty Traumatic, It Was Hilarious' – Exodus Lead Actors Talk Romance Scenes and Embodying Player Choice
articles.summary: Exodus is the upcoming Mass Effect-like sci-fi RPG, and actors Carina Conti and Stephen Oyoung reveal more about being the female and male versions of lead character Jun Aslan.
articles.body:
The voice of a main protagonist can carry a ton of weight, both for the characterization of a lead character and as the lens for which players understand a game world. Just look at the impact both Jennifer Hale and Mark Meer had on Commander Shepard in the Mass Effect series, and it's easy to see how actors are just as crucial to these games as the scripts they're given. The upcoming spacefaring sci-fi RPG Exodus seems to be taking the same approach with regard to building up its protagonist, Jun Aslan, as an avatar for players to shape through story choices and a character with a distinct personality at the same time.

On the heels of revealing the character model and voice actor for the female version of Jun , I had a conversation with both of Exodus' lead actors – Carina Conti (female Jun) and Stephen Oyoung (male Jun). We talked about the biggest differences between Exodus and their previous roles in TV shows and movies, the nuances of representing the player's choices in acting, and why Jun is important to them. But we also touch on acting out all the romance options that will be in Exodus , and the importance of having rizz . It was all fun and games with no shortage of jokes, so enjoy!

IGN: What is it about Jun that draws you now that you are on the other end of embodying this character now that you have put yourself out there as the lead for Exodus? What has been the thing that draws you to Jun?

Carina Conti: I love her [female Jun], I'm a little bit obsessed with her! She embodies qualities that I really envision for my future self. And so, getting to practice those within her over the course of six months was such a luxury. It was like, what if you already got to play this version of yourself where you are powerful, confident, and courageous, and a leader of men where you really have your ducks in a row. The great part about playing Jun, you get to play that character from every moment of that journey, building toward everything that they can become. You're already them where you take them as they as, and you're them when they become your aspirational version.

Stephen Oyoung: I think I'm just drawn to, in so many words, the hero's journey. I think Jun is fundamentally a good person thrown into these extremely challenging situations. I love that Jun is tough, but I love that Jun also feels very deeply. And that to me was one of the coolest things, to see Jun as a leader. This Jun is a fighter, but also gets heartbroken and is vulnerable enough to experience that, as well as they should, because again, the journey that Jun goes on is vast and it changes all the people and creatures around him, especially through time dilation.

IGN: One of the things you touched on, Stephen, was feeling June as a fundamentally good person and a leader. The thing is that this game has choices, so I want to talk about striking different tones – as you go through a script and have branching paths, I want to get an idea of y'all's approach to embodying those different tones for the same character. And the perspectives on how you handle different attitudes for Jun depending on player choices?

CC: I think that we all contain multitudes and we all have the potential to be one thing or another at all times, sometimes depending on how we slept that day! The actor's job is to justify the script and to justify the circumstances that were given. And so that's the greatest challenge that you can give an actor. One of them, at least, is to fundamentally be this person , but to do so in a certain kind of way – maybe in a selfish way as the character. You can choose to do these kinds of things with any line, and it's never polarized that way exactly because there's a whole spectrum, which I love about the writing in the story. That was kind of the hard work Stephen and I had to do to justify this reality.

SO: I give a massive shout out to our cinematic director Tal Peleg. He really made it very clear from day one that whatever choice you do, you have to make sure that when you are portraying that choice, you are still Jun. He cannot flip and be some completely different character. Now, I know I shot myself in the foot because I said Jun is fundamentally good! I suppose I should clarify – when I say good, it's that Jun wants what's best for Lidon [Jun's home planet], always. I spent four years on this game, so in my head I'm always thinking, 'okay, he's heroic,' but heroic can have many different shades. And sometimes that can objectively look pretty bad, so let's just rewind that before everybody at Archetype [the developer] gets on my case!

CC: It's the most relatable thing possible, which is that Jun wants the best for the people they love, you know?

SO: And how he goes about that can make him look like a boy scout or it can crash and burn, that's something for the player to see!

IGN: Of course, voice acting is in a very different realm than acting itself. Carina, a lot of your background is in TV and stage. Stephen, you've done movies and games as well. I want to talk a little bit about how different voice acting is for y'all and what served as inspiration for crafting your version of Jun, or if you just shot from the hip and said, yup, that's my Jun!

CC: I'll start by saying voice acting is really hard! It was difficult, and I would actually prefer to be on a mocap stage which I think this is one of the hardest forms of acting – you have to use so much imagination, create your own senses and memory, or whatever your process is. It's a lot of effort on the actor's part. For voice acting, I will say it's equally difficult and I certainly found it a challenge. I did my best to approach it as though I were in that space. And the reason it was difficult was because I was doing all the imaginative work of believing that I am in the space that Jun is in, believing I'm in those circumstances, believing that the stress was real, that what has been happening for the past two hours was real, and what's happening right after was real. But in reality, you are on your own in a small padded room with a microphone. So yeah, really challenging from an acting perspective.

In terms of my take on the character, I had the same approach that I have for every character, which is to find the overlap between that character and myself. That overlap can be literal, but more often it is emotional. Like, do I know what it feels like to be on my own? Do I know what it feels like to have been abandoned? Do I know what it feels like to have the odds stacked against me and have them feel insurmountable? Do I know what it feels like to be scrappy and hardworking? All those things came together to build my foundation for Jun. And those are things I hope to build within myself, which is that aspect of leadership, courage, or willingness to try new things and be brave and bold and risk it all.

SO: For me, I leaned so heavily on the writing. The writing informed everything. I knew this character had a specific background that you begin with, and after that, it just became a tight rope of wanting to give male June personality and also wanting it to be open for the player to be able to inject themselves into choices versus the player just being on rails like watching a movie unfold. I really wanted the player to feel like they were saying these lines. So every time I would have a line, I was trying my level best not to perform it as if it was a stage play, like ' watch me act! ' It was more like, I hope this is how a regular, normal person would say this in this situation.

IGN: Putting yourself out there, seeing this character in motion, and hearing yourself but having players in control of what you say – does that cross your mind? How do you feel about that unique element for this game in particular?

CC: I feel like I have to kind of emotionally sever and take a step back once my job is done. It's truly one of the greatest joys of working on a project like this. Everyone is so incredibly talented and so capable beyond what you even imagine. What they produce is, I have no words! I'm so impressed and excited. But that's like where my job ends, it's emotionally kind of where I sever it. And then the rest is just trusting everyone else to do their best. The result as far as I've seen is greater than I ever could have imagined. There is a detachment that happens, so when I see female Jun for the first time, it's really trippy. It's also like, that doesn't exactly feel like me, it's just like this very cool character that I've been part of creating, you know?

SO: This already goes to show the duality of man, we are going to be very different male and female Juns because I take everything personally! I am so invested in the success of this project in a way you would not believe! But yeah, seeing my voice on a new face is obviously unreal, super weird, but my deepest hope is that people can identify with the voice and with the face, and that they can, I guess, imprint both together, really. As far as them controlling him, I just want to see all the playthroughs because I want to see every option. I'm glad they can control me, go for it! You know, we're just actors or puppets on strings, this is what we were made for!

IGN: You two have your own way of embodying Jun with different approaches even if they're essentially the same character. But did y'all conspire with each other on how you should do certain parts, or was there any improvisation that stuck?

SO: Carina is going to get tired of hearing me say this, but we did not meet until like last week, but I think that's a good thing. It's great because I think actors should approach their character, their life with their own thing. And not telling me about it because in real life, that's how we approach other people as well. I don't know about other people's lives, so let's all just discover it together. And again, inwardly, I was competing. I am still competing with Carina! She's so cool and she kept me on my feet. Every recording session, I was thinking I must bring my A-game because I know whoever they get [for female Jun] is going to do the same. Then when I saw it was Carina, and I was like, 'okay, here we go, now we're off to the races.'

CC : You gotta be worth the investment and give it everything if you're going to do the main character twice with a branching script, make it worth it!

SO: I always say I'm a fan of Carina. I think the first time I heard her voice, there's this very special quality that Carina has where you haven't heard that kind of voice before. It's so memorable and every scene she does she knocks out of the park. And that's coming from a hater! So…now you know!

CC: I'm never going to get sick of hearing you say that! But to give Stephen his flowers as well – there were so many moments where if I was matching Steven or doing my best to match Steven's mouth movements, if the cinematic had already been rendered, instead of doing the line, I just paused and was like, 'Oh my God, Steven's voice is so beautiful.' There are different qualities in our voices, obviously naturally, but I also think based on nurture and our personalities and our backgrounds. And I think that adds something that's really unexpected for the different versions of Jun, and that's inextricable from the character experience. So, play it and find out. We're such good salesmen!

IGN: Okay, so, many of us come to these games for the romance element…

Stephen : Yes, finally, somebody asked! Alright, here we go!

IGN: So, I need to ask y'all about the romances! Take me through what it's like when you have to act out those scenes. Do you have to mentally prepare yourself, like, alright, I gotta turn my swag on, or I gotta rizz up this character?

SO: Okay, well, yes, it's all of those things. Rizz, for sure. First of all, when we're doing mocap, it's very hard to have rizz. You have a camera on your face and a skin-tight suit on. Some people are into that! But us as actors, it was very awkward but we all had a great time, it was very fun. And honestly, with something like that, there's no time to be shy. So, uh, it was very sexy and very fun. But you know, you're pantomiming. In that regard, it was actually very safe and very comfortable. Romance is a very, very fun option in this game.

CC: I will say, there was nothing sexy about my experience! It was not flattened, but it was nothing short of weird!

SO: Can I say something? The best thing that we ever did…

articles.title: Get a Free $5 Amazon Discount When You Text Alexa to Shop
articles.summary: Want a free $5 discount at Amazon? You can get one now by texting Alexa to shop.
articles.body:
The tech world is changing fast, friends. Amazon’s latest bid to get people to shop through its Alexa AI assistant is to give away free cash. Right now, if you use Alexa’s new “shop by text” ability , you can get $5 off your first order . All you have to do is text the digital assistant what you want to buy, and you’ll get the discount. You can do it here .

On that page, make sure you’re signed into your Amazon account and click the “Text Alexa” button. A box will pop up to verify the phone number associated with your account. Click “Agree and text,” and you’ll receive a text message from Alexa Shopping. Reply to that text to search for whatever ou want to buy, and you'll get an instant $5 discount.

The deal only works on items sold by Amazon and third-party sellers on the site. You can’t use it on gift cards, subscriptions, or digital content. And the promo may end at any time, so you’ll probably want to do it sooner rather than later if you’re interested in saving $5.

Texting with Alexa is just like interacting with the AI over an Echo device or using the app. You can chat with the assistant to find the item you’re looking to purchase. You can send a photo of an item to have Alexa identify it and make your purchase that way. If you need more info about this whole “texting Alexa” thing, you can probably find it on this page , which features an FAQ and has all the information about what qualifies and doesn’t for the $5 discount on your first order.

While Alexa has long been available via Echo devices and a phone app, the retailer seems to have struggled to get people to actually shop through it. Personally, I just open the Amazon app on my phone when I want to buy something at Amazon. I’ve always been wary of buying something via Alexa on my Echo because I want to verify that I’m buying the correct item, or compare prices or models. But if they’re giving away $5 discounts, I’ll probably buy the next thing I want via text.

That $5 will come in handy since Black Friday is right around the corner, and my bank account is going to take a beating. articles.title: Xbox Series X 25th Anniversary Consoles Are Arriving With Damaged Boxes for a Number of Fans
articles.summary: Microsoft's 25th anniversary translucent green Xbox Series X consoles began arriving this week for those who were able to secure one, and unfortunately a number of them are running into an all-too-common theme: a damaged box. Granted, the cardboard box on the outside is far less important than the plastic box on the inside, but with a limited-edition collectible like this – Microsoft produced just 25,000 of these X25 units – it's left some fans frustrated and disappointed.
articles.body:
Microsoft's 25th anniversary translucent green Xbox Series X consoles began arriving this week for those who were able to secure one, and unfortunately a number of them are running into an all-too-common theme: a damaged box. Granted, the cardboard box on the outside is far less important than the plastic box on the inside, but with a limited-edition collectible like this – Microsoft produced just 25,000 of these X25 units – it's left some fans frustrated and disappointed.

Longtime IGN reader Matt Fizell reached out to me directly to first flag this issue to IGN. As you can see in the photos below, his console arrived with a not-insignificant tear to the box. Matt says his order came from the Microsoft Store, which apparently didn't include any packing peanuts or other protection in the shipping box. Further exploration of this revealed other posts on X and Facebook about this, as well as an entire Reddit thread that included many others suffering from the same shipping damage. Microsoft had not responded to IGN's request for comment by the time of publication.

The 25th anniversary Xbox Series X X25 console was announced during this year's Xbox Showcase, and unsurprisingly sold out in seconds despite a retail price of $899. The translucent green controller was sold separately for those who didn't want or couldn't afford the console, but as of this writing it appears to be sold out everywhere as well. Xbox did just announce its Black Friday deals , though, if you weren't able to get your hands on the X25 console or controller.

Xbox's 25th year has been an eventful one, to say the least. Longtime Xbox boss Phil Spencer retired and was replaced by Asha Sharma, who has wasted no time in making big moves, such as slashing the price of Xbox Game Pass Ultimate , getting rid of the "This is an Xbox" marketing campaign, taking Halo away from Halo Studios and handing it to Activision , and signing Hideo Kojima's Metal Gear Solid spiritual successor Physint when Sony dropped it, among other things. Unfortunately she's also laid off thousands of people .

I wrote about my biggest memories of covering Xbox throughout its wild first quarter-century in the console business last weekend to mark the official 25th anniversary on November 15.

Ryan McCaffrey is IGN's executive editor of previews and host of IGN's weekly Xbox show, Podcast Unlocked , and a co-host of Next-Gen Console Watch . He's a North Jersey guy, so it's "Taylor ham," not "pork roll." Debate it with him on Twitter at @DMC_Ryan .

articles.title: The Hunger Games: What You Need to Know Before Sunrise on the Reaping
articles.summary: The Hunger Games: What you need to know before Sunrise on the Reaping. We break down all the characters, continuity, and Capitol shenanigans.
articles.body:
The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping opens in theaters November 20.

As with many other big movie franchises based on pre-existing stories from another medium, The Hunger Games has many fans who’ve immersed themselves in the original book series by Suzanne Collins, but also plenty of others who really only know the world via the films. And for those who’ve only engaged with its dystopian future on-screen since it was introduced in the first Hunger Games movie in 2012, you might be wondering what exactly is going on with this new installment, The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping.

Where does this sixth installment take place in the history of the series? How does it connect to the last released film, 2023’s The Hunger Games: The Ballad of Songbirds & Snakes? It’s a prequel, right, but also… Jennifer Lawrence appears in it somehow?!

Here’s your overview of the film, based on info from the previous movies and what’s been officially revealed about Sunrise on the Reaping. I won’t be giving any specific spoilers for what occurs in the book upon which it’s based, though its prequel status makes some of the big-picture spoilers more obvious since they’ve been known since the very first movie.

Sunrise on the Reaping is a prequel to the first four Hunger Games films which adapted Collins’ original three books, and takes place 24 years before we were introduced to Jennifer Lawrence’s Katniss Everdeen. Our main character here is Haymitch Abernanthy, played in the earlier films by Woody Harrelson and now portrayed as a teenager by Joseph Zada (Netflix’s East of Eden). The film depicts the 50th annual Hunger Games, which is also the second “Quarter Quell” edition. This occurs in the games every 25 years; additional twist elements are thrown in by the Capitol beyond the usual awful norm of one boy and one girl being chosen from each of the 12 districts to fight until only one of the 24 kids is left alive. The Quarter Quell concept was first depicted in Catching Fire , which took place at the 75th games and in which previous winners were brought back regardless of their age for a cruel All Stars-type edition.

We already know a few things about the 50th games from the earlier films, starting with the twist that each district had to send four children, not two — two boys and two girls. And we’ve known from the start who won those games: Haymitch, which is why he was the one and only mentor to Katniss and Peeta (Josh Hutcherson), since District 12 had no other winners who could take on that role.

This of course takes away the tension of who will survive the games in Sunrise on the Reaping, given there can only be one winner of the Hunger Games, which is why Katniss’ brave and risky move that got her and Peeta both out alive was such a big deal in the first movie. But that inherent issue is your classic prequel dilemma to solve: How do you create drama when we know the basics of the story’s outcome?

The solution that first Collins and now the filmmakers — including screenwriters Billy Ray and Michael Lesslie, and director Francis Lawrence (who’s made every Hunger Games movie except the first) — have employed is first by expanding upon who Haymitch was before the Games versus who he became after, given we were introduced to him as a bitter, sardonic drunk. And the other important element is to show the early days of the new rebellion against the Capitol that took center stage as the original films progressed, mainly by depicting several key characters in their younger days who will go on to play important roles later.

This includes previous Hunger Games winners that we saw take part in the third Quarter Quell in Catching Fire, such as Beetee (with Kelvin Harrison Jr. taking over for Jeffrey Wright), Mags (Lily Taylor taking over for Lynn Cohen), and Wiress (Maya Hawke taking over for Amanda Plummer), all of whom we know have no love for the Capitol. There are also prominent characters like Effie Trinket (Elle Fanning taking over for Elizabeth Banks) and Caesar Flickerman (Kieran Culkin taking over for Stanley Tucci) showing up in their earlier days as cogs in the Capitol’s machine, though Effie is destined to have her eyes opened to the darkness of the system she’s a part of in a way Caesar will not.

And then there’s Plutarch Heavensbee, an important figure in the Capitol who was named the head Gamemaker in Catching Fire only to turn out to be actually working against the Capitol from within, secretly helping the rebellion in crucial ways. Jesse Plemons takes on the role played by the late, great Philip Seymour Hoffman in a film that amusingly has two actors playing younger versions of men for whom they once portrayed the onscreen son — Plemons played Hoffman’s son in 2012’s The Master and Harrison Jr. played Wright’s son in 2018’s Monster.

As for the other young Tributes fighting in the Hunger Games alongside Haymitch, they include his fellow District 12 residents Maysilee (McKenna Grace), Wyatt (Ben Wang), and Louella (Molly McCann) among the 48 kids. But again, this is the Hunger Games, and Haymitch is the previously established winner, so… Well, let’s just say that if you like these guys, just be ready to be a bit (or a lot) sad about where things are going.

It was also reported a year ago by the trades and then ultimately confirmed by the actors involved that Jennifer Lawrence, Josh Hutcherson, and Woody Harrelson make appearances in this movie despite the era in which it takes place. Suffice to say, Collins’ book provided a simple way this can occur.

The most recent Hunger Games movie, 2023’s The Hunger Games: The Ballad of Songbirds & Snakes , was also a prequel but one set far earlier, during and after the events of the 10th Hunger Games that took place 64 years before Katniss’ first games.

So is there anything that happened in that movie that you should know or be reminded of for Sunrise on the Reaping? Likely not too much, given that the story was centered on the origins of the franchise’s overarching villain, Coriolanus Snow (played in the original films by the late Donald Sutherland), long before most of the other notable characters were even born. The ever-menacing Snow is also in Sunrise on the Reaping, played in his middle-aged era by Ralph Fiennes, though his screen time appears more on par with Sutherland’s as an ominous figure who pops in now and again.

Still, it’s worth brushing up on what that previous film taught us about Snow’s history in regards to District 12. That included how Snow, as a disgraced teenage boy from the Capitol (played in Songbirds & Snakes by Tom Blyth) ended up in a romantic relationship with Lucy Gray Baird (Rachel Zegler), who he had mentored in the 10th Hunger Games, where she ultimately became District 12’s first-ever winner. Even though he and Lucy Gray — who was part of District 12’s nomadic, musically-inclined group called the Covey — entertained the idea of running away together, Snow was unable to suppress his own dark inclinations and quest for power, committing heinous acts including betraying his friend to successfully get back into the Capitol's good graces. Lucy Gray’s discovery of Snow’s actions ultimately led Snow to lash out and try to kill her, shooting at her as she fled into the woods outside District 12.

Lucy Gray’s final fate is unknown, as a body is never found; it’s not clear if she died from injuries trying to escape or survived. If she survived, we don’t know if she ever returned to District 12. However, Snow’s anger at what occurred led him to suppress records of her Hunger Games; he’s unable to erase her existence but does what he can to prevent future generations knowing how District 12 came to have their first and only winner until Haymitch. And all of this also explains why he has a special scorn for District 12 and those who come from that area.

Meanwhile, Suzanne Collins has continued to be vague about Lucy Gray’s fate, even as there are many fan theories regarding her potential survival and the possibility that she had children who lived within District 12. But we know her legacy lives on in some form, as songs she wrote and performed continue to survive decades later, including “The Hanging Tree,” which Katniss sings in Mockingjay – Part 1 .

So now that we’ve gotten two prequel movies, what might be the next installment of the Hunger Games series, presuming Lionsgate wants to make more (and it’s easy to guess they will)?

That answer is unclear. So far, the movies have been strictly based on Collins’ novels, and she hasn’t released any other books since Sunrise. But the announcement that Sunrise was happening as a book was made simultaneously with the announcement of its film adaptation, showing the synergy that has risen between the two. Meanwhile, the franchise’s longtime producer and director, Nina Jacobson and Francis Lawrence, have stated they’d only want to keep making films if Collins gave them new books.

So if she were to return to Panem again, would Collins tell another prequel story or finally delve into an actual sequel? The latter raises tricky questions of whether it would diminish the ending of her book trilogy (and the four films into which it was adapted), presumably requiring some sort of big conflict to break out again à la the Star Wars sequel trilogy.

If it’s another prequel, it might be tricky now to find a story worth telling. Snow’s origins were a compelling topic, and Haymitch’s games were probably the most requested specific storyline for a prequel by fans for many years. Some always suggest going back to the very first Hunger Games, but it feels like that might not offer a lot to make it stand out, given The Ballad of Songbirds & Snakes showed us what those early, more bare-bones Hunger Games were like already. Plus, that film covered much of how the Games came to be by introducing us to Casca Highbottom (Peter Dinklage), who came up with the idea of the Hunger Games as a drunken lark only to be horrified when Snow’s father turned them into a reality.

Perhaps, though, something could be done with the first Quarter Quell, AKA the 25th Hunger Games? Now that we’ve seen the second and third “special edition” games, it does feel like we should probably fill in the gap with the first one. Also, intriguingly, almost nothing is known about that Hunger Games — including who won it! — except that the “twist” was that each district was given the awful task of voting on which of their two local children would compete and almost certainly die.

And hey, that sounds like some bleak, dystopian drama ripe for cinematic treatment!

articles.title: Gabe Newell Praised by Fans for 'Special' Way He Treats the Crew on His $500 Million Superyacht
articles.summary: Gabe Newell, the co-founder and CEO of Valve, is being praised by fans after a yacht expert took a tour of his $500 million vessel and remarked on the “special” way he treats its crew, saying it rivals anything she’s “ever seen before.”
articles.body:
Gabe Newell, the co-founder and CEO of Valve, is being praised by fans after a yacht expert took a tour of his $500 million superyacht and remarked on the “special” way he treats its crew, saying it rivals anything she’s “ever seen before.”

Gabe Newell is the proud owner of a $500 million superyacht named the Leviathan. It’s 111 meters long and boasts a few key features that were designed with its crew in mind. For example, it has a massive gaming center where guests, the owner, and staff can play video games together, as well as swanky VIP cabins that the crew can use if needed. They even have their own sleek, stylish rooms reserved just for employees, as well as swimming pools where they can receive their diving certifications. Gabe even commissioned a special glass panel engraved with the names of every person involved in the ship's design and construction.

Even the yacht’s flooring was intended to give the crew a break, ditching teak and wood in favor of a material that’s easier to clean. As told by Francesca Webster of the SuperYacht Times, it’s “a lot more functional for the crew, easy to clean, and gives them more time to do experiences with the owner and the guests on board.”

Photos From Gabe Newell's $500 Million Superyacht 'Leviathan'

Webster took a tour of the Leviathan for a video on the SuperYacht Times’ YouTube channel, where she remarked on how well Newell treats his staff and how unusual this is in the yachting business.

“Gabe actually opted to utilize this incredible space for the crew mess. He eats with the crew every day. They enjoy their meals together. It’s all about shared experience on board his boat. That’s something that we’ve really never seen before in our industry,” Webster said of the main deck saloon. She also revealed that Newell manages to keep staff for more than four and a half years — far more than the average superyacht staff retention of six to nine months.

The video quickly went viral, earning no shortage of praise from fans who couldn’t help but wonder how grim things in the yachting world must be if Newell is truly turning it on its head by treating his employees like equals.

“‘He has a different perspective on interacting with the people on board’ — SuperYacht enjoyer describing someone who doesn’t hate people,” one commenter joked on YouTube.

“This entire video is, ‘It astonishes me that Gabe actually cares about his crew and treats them as people. It’s so rare to see an owner who respects humans around them,’” another said.

“The fact this is such an outrageous world- first that the crew is seen as actual people tells you all you need to know,” another wrote.

This isn't the only big purchase from Newell to make headlines; earlier this year, Newell purchased a $70.8 million mansion in Manalapan, Florida that comes with a dock and boat lift for his yacht, an in-ground pool, an eight-car garage, and even an underground tunnel that leads out to an adjoining beach.

This is one of the more recent insights we’ve gotten into the life of Gabe Newell after a Counter-Strike ’s co-creator revealed that Newell got so obsessed with Mongolian Throat singing at one point that employees would close their office doors to muffle the sound of him practicing in Valve’s corporate headquarters.
